title: How do you playtest your games? It's hard to make a good game without playtests!
author: zavtraleto
selftext:
**How do you playtest your games?**

I've made one of my first games to a fairly playable state (beta? alpha?), and now I'm trying to figure out how well it actually plays. But how to understand how players approach it and identify what needs improving?  
  
What's your approach to playtesting? Do you go with friends & family? Discord communities where developers exchange playtests? Maybe we have something similar here? Maybe make a public demo and share it on itch.io?

I've just reached the first alpha/beta stage of my little puzzle game (if you have a minute give it a try here: [VIZAVI](https://playgama.com/game/vizavi)), and I'm interested in feedback on the gameplay, level design, and overall feel.

The problem is - when you're the one making and playing the game over and over, it's incredibly hard to judge it! You become too good at it!

I'm interested in your approaches and stories!

comments.author: AshlaStudios
comments.body: First off you need to realize who your target audience is. Hopefully you have one. Focus tests are most valuable and important early on. If you know anyone who plays the kind of game you're making, invite them for like full day playtests and just watch how they react, ask them to be brutally honest. If you don't know anyone, search for online communities of games with your target audience. Pay them if you have to. You are correct, playtesting is really, really important and devs with no experience often realize this way too late.

comments.author: Carter5on
comments.body:
I play the game over and over again for many hours. In your case, I would go with an itchio Demo. I have noticed people are more vocal there.  
  
I stopped at Level 8. I understand that maybe you want it to be challenging, but I would love if I could jump diagonally too. It has a nice aesthetic. The mechanic reminds me of Bloxorz.

replies.author: zavtraleto
replies.body: Thank you so much for your feedback! I'll try it on itch. Yep, I want to make a puzzle game that gets more and more challenging, and level design is very interesting and is pretty hard to do.

replies.author: Carter5on
replies.body: Another way is to give Claude access to your game's folder on desktop. You need to download the desktop version of Claude. When it has access, you ask it to play your game and you describe what you want it to look our for, what to test, etc.

comments.author: Arkenhammer
comments.body: We do our early play testing at game dev meetups and other local game focused events.

comments.author: DigitalDustChan
comments.body: I built an agent playtester and it's been playing my game with itself for a while now. My daughter asks me what my computer is doing sometimes and I tell her that my AI is playing games with itself.

replies.author: zavtraleto
replies.body: I've tried to do so. Agents are good for testing mechanics, but in my opinion, they couldn't properly test level design, emotional part of a game, the progression, the experience and the FUN. Agents totally don't get the FUN part

replies.author: DigitalDustChan
replies.body:
Well... if they did it wouldn't really be your game, would it? My playtester tests for traversal errors, glitches, and bugs. If you want to offload fun then why even build a game?

I think the answer to your question is that you can build everything else at 20x speed, but you're going to have to use 1x speed to measure and refine fun. Personally, I find it a lot easier to get to the fun if all the auxiliary bugs are smoothed out of the way first.

comments.author: lawlshawk
comments.body:
honestly what's worked for me is a private itch page in restricted mode ... you hand out download keys so only people you invite get in, and you can revoke a key anytime. started with 3 friends and it's around 20 testers now

  
the bigger thing is building feedback in from day 0. in-game survey + some lightweight telemetry (where they die / quit / how long a run takes) so you're not relying on people remembering. people will say "it was fine" while the data shows exactly where they stopped

  
for a puzzle game i'd log time per level + restarts per level, that's basically your difficulty curve for free

  
and agree agents don't get the fun part ... they're good for catching breakage, you still need humans for the fun

comments.author: office-canard
comments.body: If you can't find testers, you have to do it yourself. What I do is mess with my own condition. I play after a few drinks, half distracted while doing something else, or right after waking up. You stop being "too good at it" pretty quickly that way.

comments.author: SpaceTradeCompany
comments.body: I created a decision table so I can play test against computer. But I have also play tested with friends and family a lot, since i have developed an android app, you need friends and family as beta testers to get it out on google play.
